questions.statement: Which sentence uses an It-cleft to put the focus on the time?
questions.context: A news report in Cartago described when the main road reopened after the floods.

options.text: It was after the floods that the road to Cartago reopened.
options.feedback: This works: It was ... that isolates the time phrase, so the sentence stresses when the road reopened.

options.text: The road to Cartago reopened after the floods, as everyone knows.
options.feedback: This is a plain declarative with an added comment, so no element is singled out for emphasis here.

options.text: After the floods, the road to Cartago reopened last Saturday.
options.feedback: This is normal word order with the cause in front, so the sentence stresses the floods, not the time.

options.text: The floods made the road to Cartago reopen a little later.
options.feedback: This presents the floods as the cause in an ordinary causal sentence, not in an emphasis structure.

questions.explanation:
An It-cleft splits a clause into It was plus a focus plus that plus the rest, so one element becomes the topic.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which closing is the correct one for that formal email?
questions.context: Daniela is writing a formal email to the principal of her school in Heredia.

options.text: Love, Dani
options.feedback: Love is a friendly sign-off used between close peers, so it does not fit a formal email to a principal.

options.text: Catch you later, Daniela
options.feedback: This is an informal goodbye between friends, so it sounds far too casual for official school business.

options.text: Yours sincerely, Daniela Vargas
options.feedback: This works: Yours sincerely is a standard formal valediction and it is followed by the writer's full name.

options.text: Thanks for everything, Dani
options.feedback: This thanks the reader but it is not a closing formula, so the email would end with no proper sign-off.

questions.explanation:
Formal letters and emails close with a valediction such as Yours sincerely, followed by the writer's full name and surname.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which version correctly inverts the subject and the auxiliary verb?
questions.context: A teacher in San Jose explained why the students stayed after the last bell.

options.text: Only after the last bell the students did leave the building.
options.feedback: Here the auxiliary did stays after the subject, but a fronted phrase at the start forces inversion.

options.text: Only after the last bell did the students leave the building.
options.feedback: This works: the fronted phrase comes first, so the auxiliary did moves in front of the subject.

options.text: After the last bell only did the students leave the building.
options.feedback: Only is misplaced inside the time phrase, so the fronted element is not the one that triggers inversion.

options.text: Only after the last bell did leave the students the building.
options.feedback: The verb is cut off from its subject by the object here, so this is not the inverted clause at all.

questions.explanation:
When a phrase such as only after the last bell opens the sentence, the auxiliary comes before the subject.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence shows results improving as practice increases?
questions.context: Daniela trains at the track in Cartago and wants to show how practice changes her times.

options.text: She trains more, so she runs faster every single morning.
options.feedback: So links two separate facts, so it gives a result without showing how the two amounts depend on each other.

options.text: The more she trains, faster she runs on the track.
options.feedback: The first half is right, but the correlative needs a second the before the comparative in the other clause.

options.text: She trains the most, so she runs the fastest every morning.
options.feedback: The superlative compares her with everyone, while the context describes how her own effort changes her speed.

options.text: The more she trains, the faster she runs on the track.
options.feedback: This works: the pair the more and the faster links two clauses whose quantities grow together.

questions.explanation:
The correlative pair the more and the is used when one quantity rises and another rises or falls with it.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence best gives the main idea of that radio piece?
questions.context: A short radio piece said that Alajuela recycled thirty percent more glass this year.

options.text: Glass recycling in Alajuela went up this year.
options.feedback: This works: it keeps the topic, the place and the general trend, which is exactly what a main idea needs.

options.text: A radio station in Alajuela got new equipment this year.
options.feedback: The station and its equipment are only background in the report, so this moves away from the main topic.

options.text: Alajuela residents must separate glass before Friday.
options.feedback: No deadline is heard on the air, so this adds a rule and turns a reported fact into invented advice.

options.text: Alajuela will open a new recycling plant next year.
options.feedback: A future plant is never announced, so this invents a development the report does not support at all.

questions.explanation:
A main idea keeps the central topic and general trend, while names, figures and side remarks belong to the details.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which detail did the guest give about that recycling drive?
questions.context: In a podcast from Alajuela the guest named the school that joined a recycling drive.

options.text: The drive collected paper from every household in the country.
options.feedback: This names every household in the country, but the guest only mentioned one school taking part.

options.text: The Liceo de Alajuela joined the recycling drive.
options.feedback: This works: it repeats the specific detail given on air, the name of the school that joined the drive.

options.text: The drive started after the mayor visited a school.
options.feedback: A visit by the mayor never appears in the podcast, so this adds a cause that was not stated.

options.text: The drive ended last March with no results at all.
options.feedback: The guest described a drive that was still going on, so this adds an ending date and a negative result.

questions.explanation:
Listening for details means catching the exact names, figures and times that support the general point of a report.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence works best as the thesis of an opinion essay?
questions.context: Andres must write an opinion essay about public transport for his school in Alajuela.

options.text: In this essay I am going to talk about several things.
options.feedback: This only announces the topic, so it makes no claim and gives no reason a reader could argue with.

options.text: Public transport is nice and everybody knows that.
options.feedback: The vague adjective and everybody knows weaken the claim, so it is not a thesis a reader can test.

options.text: I walked to school yesterday and it took twenty minutes.
options.feedback: This is a personal anecdote about one morning, so it supports no general position on transport.

options.text: In my opinion, buses should run more often, because many students arrive late.
options.feedback: This works: it states a clear opinion and because introduces the reason the essay will develop.

questions.explanation:
A thesis is one clear argument plus the reason for it; an introduction should not only announce a topic or tell a story.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses inversion correctly after a negative adverb?
questions.context: A coach in Heredia was describing what her athletes achieved last spring.

options.text: Rarely have our athletes trained as hard as they did last spring.
options.feedback: This works: rarely is a negative adverb, so the auxiliary have moves in front of the subject our athletes.

options.text: Rarely our athletes have trained as hard as they did last spring.
options.feedback: The subject sits between rarely and the auxiliary, so the inversion that rarely requires never happens.

options.text: Rarely have trained our athletes as hard as they did last spring.
options.feedback: The verb appears before its subject here, so the clause is not the subject-auxiliary order that rarely needs.

options.text: Rarely did trained our athletes as hard as they did last spring.
options.feedback: Did with the past participle leaves no place for the subject, so the auxiliary form is wrong as well.

questions.explanation:
Negative adverbs at the start of a sentence, such as rarely or not only, invert the subject and the auxiliary.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence makes the best topic sentence for that paragraph?
questions.context: In an essay about coffee in Turrialba, Sofia is writing the second body paragraph.

options.text: To conclude, coffee farming in Turrialba has a bright future.
options.feedback: To conclude only fits the last paragraph, so this sentence cannot introduce the ideas of a body paragraph.

options.text: For example, one farmer near the volcano earns half his income from sales.
options.feedback: For example opens a supporting detail, so it belongs after the main point of the paragraph has been stated.

options.text: A second serious problem for small growers is the low price they receive.
options.feedback: This works: it names the second main idea of the essay and announces the reasons that will follow.

options.text: On the other hand, my cousin prefers tea to coffee in the morning.
options.feedback: This switches to a personal preference the essay never argues about, so it breaks the paragraph's topic.

questions.explanation:
Each body paragraph states one main idea first, then supports it with examples, data or reasons.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence makes that request politely in a formal email?
questions.context: Kevin needs to ask the coordinator in Cartago for a change of class hour.

options.text: You must change my class hour to the afternoon, right now.
options.feedback: You must plus the bare command is an order, so it sounds demanding in a request to a coordinator.

options.text: I would like to request a change of my class hour, if possible.
options.feedback: This works: would like to request is a polite formula, and if possible softens the demand even further.

options.text: Change my class hour to the afternoon, no problem?
options.feedback: An imperative plus a tag question demands action here, so the tone is rude rather than courteous.

options.text: I need you to change my hour, so do it soon, please.
options.feedback: So do it soon gives a direct command, so adding please cannot cancel that forceful order.

questions.explanation:
Formal requests use hedged forms such as would like to request or could you possibly, never bare imperatives.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Rewrite it so that the focus falls on the volunteer brigade?
questions.context: In Escazu the volunteer brigade fixed the broken water pipes last week.

options.text: It was last week when the volunteer brigade fixed the broken pipes.
options.feedback: This is a time cleft, so it emphasises last week and leaves the doer in the background clause.

options.text: What the volunteer brigade fixed were the broken pipes in Escazu.
options.feedback: A what cleft here puts the pipes in the focus slot, so the brigade is not the stressed element.

options.text: It was the volunteer brigade that fixed the broken pipes in Escazu.
options.feedback: This works: It was plus the agent plus that lifts the doer into the focus, as the question asks.

options.text: The broken pipes were fixed in Escazu by the volunteer brigade.
options.feedback: This is the passive voice, which moves the doer away from the focus instead of stressing it.

questions.explanation:
Cleft sentences divide one clause into two so a chosen element becomes the focus, as in It was the brigade that fixed them.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What can you reasonably infer from what the guide said?
questions.context: In an interview a Heredia guide said tours are booked out three weeks ahead every July.

options.text: July is the busiest month for tours to Heredia.
options.feedback: This works: if July tours fill three weeks ahead, demand in that month must be high, so it is the peak.

options.text: Heredia has closed its tourism office for good.
options.feedback: Nothing about a permanent closure appears in the interview, so this goes far beyond what was said.

options.text: Fewer than ten tourists visited Heredia last July.
options.feedback: Advance bookings signal many visitors rather than fewer than ten, so this contradicts the evidence.

options.text: Tours to Heredia in July are free of charge.
options.feedback: The guide never mentions prices at all, so no conclusion about free entry can be drawn from bookings.

questions.explanation:
A safe inference stays inside the evidence: from booking three weeks ahead we may conclude high demand, never prices.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence about those trails is completely correct?
questions.context: A travel brochure compares the three longest trails around Monteverde for visitors.

options.text: This is the more long trail of the three, so it also takes the most time.
options.feedback: Double comparatives collide here, since more long and the most describe the same item in one sentence.

options.text: The Chompipe trail is the most steep of those three routes.
options.feedback: A superlative takes the most plus an adjective, not most plus an adverb, so this form is wrong.

options.text: The Chompipe trail takes more hours than any other trail there.
options.feedback: Any other already means most of all, so it wrongly replaces the comparative form more hours.

options.text: The Chompipe trail is by far the steepest of the three trails.
options.feedback: This works: by far strengthens the superlative and steepest already carries the final -est ending.

questions.explanation:
Superlatives take the most or the least plus a short adjective, or add -est, and modifiers such as by far raise the degree.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which rewrite keeps the request but fixes the register problem?
questions.context: A draft email to the principal of a Limon school reads: Hey, send me the report, thanks.

options.text: Hey, send me that report now, thanks a lot, bye.
options.feedback: The informal tone stays and the command grows stronger, so the message still fails school protocol.

options.text: Dear Principal, could you please send me the report at your convenience?
options.feedback: This works: the formal greeting plus could you please turns the demand into a courteous hedged request.

options.text: Hey, just send the report, ok? I need it.
options.feedback: Just and ok keep the message casual and demanding, so the register is informal in a formal email.

options.text: Hello teacher, send me the report quick, thanks.
options.feedback: Quick is informal and demands a fast order, so it clashes with the polite tone a school email requires.

questions.explanation:
Formal email keeps a respectful greeting and hedged verbs such as could or would; slang and bare imperatives do not.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence presents a counterargument fairly in an opinion essay?
questions.context: In Cartago, Mariela must present the opposite view before defending her position on uniforms.

options.text: School uniforms are the worst idea anyone has ever had.
options.feedback: This is an insult with no argument, so it dismisses the other side instead of presenting it for the reader.

options.text: Critics say uniforms hide identity, although most students still prefer them.
options.feedback: The connector although sets up a contrast, so the writer's own preference replaces the claim being explained.

options.text: Some people argue that uniforms limit self-expression, yet they also save time.
options.feedback: This works: some people argue states the opposing view and yet adds the writer's reply in one sentence.

options.text: Those who dislike uniforms simply have no taste at all.
options.feedback: This attacks the people instead of their idea, so it is personal and never answers the argument.

questions.explanation:
A counterargument is stated fairly with hedges like some people argue, then answered with a contrast such as yet.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which order makes that paragraph clearest for the reader?
questions.context: A Puntarenas paragraph mixes four sentences: A the dry season lasts, B farmers plant, C rains came late, D harvests shrank.

options.text: B, A, C, D
options.feedback: Starting with the planting detail leaves the reader without the seasonal frame the rest of the text explains.

options.text: C, D, A, B
options.feedback: The result comes before the background that explains it, so the reader meets the consequence before its reason.

options.text: D, C, B, A
options.feedback: This puts the effect before its cause and ends on the driest fact, so the logic runs backwards.

options.text: A, C, D, B
options.feedback: This works: general season, then the problem, then its result, then the human response, a clean chain.

questions.explanation:
A well-linked paragraph moves from general background to the specific problem, then to its result and the consequences.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which rewrite really stresses that the team won the final?
questions.context: The volleyball team in Alajuela won the final last Saturday at the school gym.

options.text: It was last Saturday that the team in Alajuela won the final.
options.feedback: This is a time cleft, so it stresses last Saturday and leaves the winning itself in the background.

options.text: What the team in Alajuela did was win the final last Saturday.
options.feedback: This works: a what cleft with did was puts the action win in the focus slot, so the victory is stressed.

options.text: The team in Alajuela won the final last Saturday at the gym.
options.feedback: This is plain word order with the time first, so it stresses the date rather than the victory.

options.text: It was the final that the team in Alajuela won last Saturday.
options.feedback: This is an object cleft, so it stresses the final itself instead of the act of winning it.

questions.explanation:
To stress the action itself use a what cleft, as in What they did was win; time and object clefts move the focus elsewhere.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which reply disagrees politely and still gives a clear reason?
questions.context: At a debate in Cartago, Gabriel must disagree with a classmate who praised group work.

options.text: No, group work is useless and you clearly did not understand it.
options.feedback: No plus useless attacks the other speaker, so the disagreement is rude and it offers no usable reason.

options.text: You are completely wrong about group work, sorry, but that is all.
options.feedback: The insult cancels the apology and the reason given is empty, so the reply fails on tone and on content.

options.text: I see your point, but in our group the work was divided badly, so I prefer working alone.
options.feedback: This works: the concession I see your point softens the refusal, and but plus so carries the reason.

options.text: Group work is better, obviously, so stop complaining about it.
options.feedback: This agrees with the classmate instead of disagreeing, so it does not do what the speaker was asked to do.

questions.explanation:
Polite disagreement needs a concession, a contrast such as but and a reason; attacking the person breaks the discussion.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which conclusion does that comparison support, and no more?
questions.context: A report said forty percent of the Heredia buses were late in May, against twenty-five in April.

options.text: Bus delays in Heredia were worse in May than they were in April.
options.feedback: This works: forty percent is above twenty-five, so the report supports exactly this claim about those two months.

options.text: Most buses in Heredia run late in every month of the year.
options.feedback: Two months of figures cannot prove a pattern for the whole year, so this generalises far beyond the data.

options.text: The buses in Heredia need to be replaced immediately.
options.feedback: A rise in delays never proves that vehicles must be replaced, so this recommendation goes beyond the evidence.

options.text: April was the worst month of the year for transport.
options.feedback: The report compares April and May only, so it cannot rank April against every other month of the year.

questions.explanation:
A justified conclusion stays inside the data: comparing two months supports a claim about those months only, not the year.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which version is fully correct in register, structure and verb forms?
questions.context: A student wrote this draft email to the director of a college in Puntarenas.

options.text: Hey you, the new timetable is not more better than the last one, ok?
options.feedback: The informal greeting and not more better both fail: a double comparative cannot stand and the tone is wrong too.

options.text: Dear Director, the new timetable is better and it fits better, students will like it.
options.feedback: Two complete clauses are joined with only a comma here, so the sentence fuses and the email loses its finish.

options.text: Dear Director, which starts at seven, the new timetable suits working students best.
options.feedback: The relative clause which starts at seven has no subject to attach to, so it dangles before the main clause.

options.text: Dear Director, I am writing to explain why the new timetable suits students better than the old one.
options.feedback: This works: a formal greeting, a clear purpose and one comparative clause make the email correct and polite.

questions.explanation:
A formal email needs a respectful greeting, one clear purpose and one idea per sentence; comma splices and dangling relatives break it.
